content: Elderberry, also known as Elder, belongs to the genus Sambucus, which comprises between 5 and 30 species of shrubs or small trees, with two species being herbaceous. Historically, these plants were classified under the honeysuckle family (Caprifoliaceae), but genetic evidence has since reclassified them into the moschatel family (Adoxaceae). The genus Sambucus is native to temperate and subtropical regions of both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. However, it is more prevalent in the Northern Hemisphere, with its Southern Hemisphere distribution limited to parts of Australasia and South America. The leaves of elderberry plants are arranged oppositely and are pinnate, typically consisting of 5 to 9 leaflets (though occasionally 3 or 11). Each leaf measures 5–30 cm in length, and the leaflets have serrated edges. During late spring, elderberry plants produce large clusters of small white or cream-colored flowers, which are followed by clusters of small berries. These berries can be red, bluish, or black, and less commonly yellow or white. The lifespan of elderberry species ranges from 80 to 100 years. Elderberries serve as an important food source for many bird species. Additionally, elder plants are utilized as host plants by the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including the Brown-tail, Buff Ermine, Dot Moth, Emperor Moth, The Engrailed, Swallow-tailed Moth, and The V-pug. The crushed foliage and unripe fruit of elderberry plants emit a strong, unpleasant odor. Dead elderwood is a preferred habitat for the fungus Auricularia auricula-judae, commonly known as Judas' ear fungus. In California, the Valley elderberry longhorn beetle is frequently found around red or blue elderberry bushes. Female beetles lay their eggs on the bark, and the larvae hatch and burrow into the stems of the plant. Species Groups The common elder complex is often treated as a single species, Sambucus nigra, which is found in the warmer regions of Europe and North America. This species has several regional varieties or subspecies, or it may be considered a group of closely related species. The flowers of this group are arranged in flat corymbs, and the berries are black to glaucous blue. These plants are larger shrubs, reaching heights of 5–8 meters, and occasionally grow into small trees up to 15 meters tall with stem diameters of up to 30–60 cm. Other notable species include: Sambucus australis (Southern Elder): Found in temperate eastern South America. Sambucus canadensis (American Elder): Found in eastern North America, with blue-black berries. Sambucus cerulea (Blueberry Elder): Found in western North America, with blue berries. Sambucus javanica (Chinese Elder): Found in southeastern Asia. Sambucus mexicana (Mexican Elder): Found in Mexico and Central America, with blue-black berries. Sambucus nigra (Black Elder): Found in Europe and western Asia, with black berries. Sambucus palmensis (Canary Islands Elder): Found in the Canary Islands, with black berries. Sambucus peruviana (Peruvian Elder): Found in northwest South America, with black berries. Sambucus simpsonii (Florida Elder): Found in southeastern United States, with blue-black berries. Sambucus velutina (Velvet Elder): Found in southwestern North America, with blue-black berries. The red-berried elder complex is often treated as a single species, Sambucus racemosa, found throughout the colder regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The flowers are arranged in rounded panicles, and the berries are bright red. These are smaller shrubs, rarely exceeding 3–4 meters in height. Notable species in this group include: Sambucus callicarpa (Pacific Coast Red Elder): Found on the west coast of North America. Sambucus pubens (American Red Elder): Found in northern North America. Sambucus racemosa (European Red Elder): Found in northern Europe and northwest Asia. Sambucus sieboldiana (Japanese Red Elder): Found in Japan and Korea. The Australian elder group consists of two species from Australasia. These plants produce flowers in rounded panicles and have white or yellow berries. They are shrubs that grow up to 3 meters in height. Uses Both the flowers and berries of elderberry plants can be used to produce elderberry wine. In Hungary, elderberry brandy is made, requiring 50 kg of fruit to produce 1 liter of brandy. The alcoholic drink sambuca is created by infusing elderberries and anise into alcohol. Elderberries should not be consumed raw, as they are mildly toxic and can cause vomiting, particularly if eaten unripe. The mild cyanide toxicity present in the berries is destroyed through cooking. Cooked berries can be used to make jam, pies, or Pontack sauce. All green parts of the plant are poisonous, containing cyanogenic glycosides. Elderflowers can be used to make herbal tea, which is believed to help alleviate colds and fevers. In Europe, elderflowers are often made into a syrup or cordial, which is diluted with water before drinking. This traditional drink has gained popularity, leading to the commercial production of elderflower-flavored soft drinks, such as Fanta Shokata. Elderflowers can also be used to make a mildly alcoholic, sparkling elderflower champagne. Several clinical studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of Sambucol, a formulation based on elderberry extract, in treating influenza types A and B in both adults and children. Sambucol has been shown to reduce the severity and duration of flu symptoms in otherwise healthy individuals. However, it should not be considered a substitute for influenza vaccination, particularly in high-risk individuals. An in vitro study of Sambucol also suggested potential effectiveness against the H5N1 avian influenza virus. Folklore In folklore, elder trees were considered unlucky to have in a garden. Cutting down an elder tree was believed to release a spirit known as the Elder Mother, who would take revenge. This belief is reflected in a line from the Wiccan Rede: Elder be the Lady's tree, burn it not or cursed you'll be. This superstition may have originated from ancient Pagan beliefs, which regarded the elder tree as sacred to the Moon Goddess. It was thought that the tree could only be safely cut while chanting a rhyme to the Elder Mother. Trivia The box elder is not an elder at all but is an alternative name for the Manitoba Maple.
